title: Conversation stitching and reusable KV anchors
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: many requests share overlapping leading context (system prompts, user profile snippets, onboarding shells). These lead to duplicated KV storage across GPU slabs, increasing GPU memory pressure and reducing effective throughput. Existing per-request prefix fingerprinting reduces some duplication but misses convergent-but-not-identical sequences (minor token differences, templated slots) and does not provide a stable anchor object that can be referenced across requests.

Goals: 1) Reduce redundant KV residency by introducing reusable, referencable KV anchors (stable prefix segments) that multiple requests can point to. 2) Integrate anchors with continuous batching so requests that share anchors are co-located on the same GPU for immediate reuse. 3) Provide safe merge/consolidation of near-duplicate anchors to reclaim memory without regressing quality. 4) Maintain per-tenant isolation and predictable eviction behavior.

Proposal overview: 1) Anchor extraction: run a lightweight normalization pass on incoming prompts to identify candidate anchor segments (leading tokens up to configurable length or up to separator token). Normalize templates (strip variable slots), canonicalize whitespace, and compute an anchor signature using a combination of short rolling hash + minimizer sketch (to make near-duplicates converge). 2) Anchor registry: maintain a per-tenant anchor index mapping signature -> anchor_id; entries store metadata as a compact header (length, token-count, model-compatibility mask, refcount, last-used timestamp). The registry is persisted in the control-plane DB and a GPU-resident compact ledger (cache) for fast lookup. 3) Anchor materialization and storage: anchors correspond to a contiguous KV slice (or set of slices) stored in GPU slabs. When an anchor is newly materialized, it is allocated from a shared anchor slab allocator (slabs optimized for read-sharing). Anchors are reference-counted; requests include anchor_id in the serving RPC so the runtime can attach the preloaded KV pointer to the generation pipeline. 4) Merge/consolidation service: a background worker periodically scans the registry for near-duplicate anchors using LSH + token edit distance thresholds. Merge candidates are validated by a lightweight eval harness that samples a small set of prompts and ensures logits/outputs deviation within configured tolerance. Successful merges produce a canonical anchor_id, update registry refs, and schedule the old anchor slices for reclamation. 5) Placement and batching: to maximize reuse, the router uses an anchor-aware heuristic: prefer routing requests with hot anchors to GPUs where the anchor KV is resident. If strict latency SLOs prevent optimal placement, router falls back to nearest available variant and triggers async prefetch of anchor to local GPU. Batching scheduler coalesces requests sharing anchor_id into the same micro-batch to avoid repeated KV loads. 6) Eviction and lifecycle: anchors have a two-tier eviction policy: soft TTL + LRU for low-value anchors, and pinned anchors for enterprise customers. Eviction is refcount-aware and will consolidate low-refcount anchors before evicting highly shared ones. 7) Migration/fallback: for compatibility with older runtimes or with models that cannot reuse anchor slices (e.g., different kv-layout), anchor_id will be ignored and the request will proceed with standard prefix append. We keep canonical fallback metrics to track missed reuse.

Metrics and success criteria: - GPU KV memory reduction: target 20-40% in workloads with high prefix overlap (benchmarked with internal conversational workloads). - Token-generation p95 latency overhead: <5% added for anchor lookup + potential prefetch. - Anchor hit rate: target >=60% for enterprise conversational customers and >=30% on mixed workloads. - Merge false-positive rate: <1% (as measured by eval harness).

Rollout plan: alpha behind feature flag for 5 internal tenants -> canary to 10 customers with opt-in -> broad rollout. We'll gate on memory savings and p95 latency in the canary.

Trade-offs and risks: - Risk of subtle output drift if anchor consolidation merges sequences with small but important differences; mitigated by conservative merge thresholds and pre-merge eval sampling. - Router complexity increases (placement by anchor): mitigated via progressive rollout and monitoring. - Extra control-plane state for anchors increases operational surface; we will shard registry by tenant and implement eviction/compaction tasks.

Open questions: - Best normalization heuristics for templated prompts across customers (we should A/B different normalizers). - Exact merge thresholds and eval-sample size that balance savings vs risk. - How to charge customers for pinned anchors (cost model for Dedicated/Private?).
